pull.title: net: reimplement private broadcast as jobs isolated from the node
pull.body:
Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to
the connection manager. Each job runs on its own thread, shares no state with the node, and
reaches the network only through the Tor proxy: it resolves the chain's DNS seeds, then announces
over BIP324 to recipients on a schedule drawn up front, each connection with fresh isolation
credentials. Nothing a recipient does, and nothing the node sees of the transaction coming back,
changes the plan, and the transaction enters the node's mempool only when it returns from the
network. The old private broadcast connections and relay are removed.

The invariants are specified in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`.

The rest of the tests are in a follow-up to be considered later:
https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup

This PR's tests do not check that each attempt gets its own VERSION nonce, PING nonce and BIP324 key (A4 in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`), so a regression there would pass.

On 19f9cd7c4d I made each of these values a constant for the whole process, one line in `src/privbcast/attempt.cpp` at a time. All four `p2p_private_broadcast*.py` tests passed on each of the three variants. Constant proxy credentials, by contrast, make `p2p_private_broadcast.py` fail.

Your [follow-up branch](https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup) already checks all three, in `p2p_private_broadcast_job.py`; I ran it on the PING-nonce variant and it fails there. A reused nonce or key lets recipients link a node's broadcasts to each other, the same kind of leak as the IP linkage the kept tests guard against. Could that check move into this PR?

@fametrano willing to be convinced to move particular items to this PR, but I'm really focusing on IP address level leaks for the first PR. Preventing cross-attempt or cross-tx fingerprinting is a secondary goal, and hard to achieve arbitrary level of assurances, hence its deferral. 

edit: changed my mind and brought it forward

I find the following not acceptable:

Relying on DNS seeds
--------------------

Currently DNS seeds are used only to bootstrap a new node. That happens once in its lifetime and there is a fallback mechanism if the DNS seeds do not work. We never rely solely only on DNS seeds for something. They are centralized services.

`doc/dnsseed-policy.md` mentions:

> Bitcoin Core attempts to minimize the level of trust in DNS seeds

I do not think that it is reasonable to start relying on a few servers permanently (not just once in a lifetime, but every time a node wants to privately broadcast a transaction). This means that if a few operators decide to switch off (or misbehave) their services then everybody on the network is obstructed from privately broadcasting their transactions. That resembles more a client-server architecture than a decentralized P2P network.

Not broadcasting to Tor or I2P peers
------------------------------------

Only broadcasting to IP peers via the Tor network would make the feature too fragile - it would rely on the Tor network and the Tor exit nodes working properly. The Tor network has been down in the past. I think it is important to have a fallback mechanism which currently is the I2P network. Also, right now we do not rely on the Tor exit nodes. We could broadcast a transaction within the Tor network to an `.onion` peer even if the exit nodes are off or misbehaving.

Even moderate adoption of private broadcast in its current form improves the privacy of everybody because everybody could be a recipient. Privacy is improved even for nodes that broadcast-to-all. That would be spoiled if we only send to IP peers. Note that a private broadcast recipient would further broadcast-to-all the newly received transaction in a way that is indistinguishable from them being the transaction originator. So an observer can no longer tell whether a node is the original sender or was a recipient of a private broadcast. For this to work everybody must be a potential private broadcast recipient.

> I do not think that it is reasonable to start relying on a few servers permanently (not just once in a lifetime, but every time a node wants to privately broadcast a transaction). This means that if a few operators decide to switch off (or misbehave) their services then everybody on the network is obstructed from privately broadcasting their transactions. That resembles more a client-server architecture than a decentralized P2P network.

If the seeds go offline, private broadcast stops; it doesn't leak. If they misbehave, the most they can do is pick recipients that drop the transaction. They can't learn who is sending. 

The alternative of picking Tor/i2p peers from addrman as master does, is not an answer anyone should be happy with.

Today we give attackers significant influence over choices being made by victim. Peers can be influenced, by design, into dialing to peers that are unique fingerprints, with the attacker writing to their addrman.

Tor isn't decentralized either, but we accept utility in terms of privacy.

> I think it is important to have a fallback mechanism which currently is the I2P network. 

Currently in master, it makes sybiling victims much easier, which results in an IP address leak, which is an unfortunate side-effect of the current architecture. Assuming we adopted something like this PR, then we would have to introduce a "just in time" gathering of addresses, which would *still* be going through seeder nodes, or again, reintroducing fundamental leaks via local addrman usage. No free lunch here.

> Even moderate adoption of private broadcast in its current form improves the privacy of everybody because everybody could be a recipient. Privacy is improved even for nodes that broadcast-to-all. 

The attacks it resists are quite limited today, and therefore it's sort of in purgatory where we can't make any promises about it. That's quite sad, and completely avoidable.

The design doc looks AI written; is it meant for human or agentic consumption? Shouldn't it be a BIP, or at least posted to the mailing list for broader discussion on exactly the sort of tradeoffs vasild raises [above](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6413061893)?

+6k lines (+3.5k -1k under src excluding test) seems like a lot. Presumably also AI written with light human review?

If the idea is to separate this from the node, it seems like having a separate binary interacting lightly with the node might be a better structure. Something like: a "bitcoin-privbcast" binary, connects only over i2p/tor, keeps it own addrman independent from the node, initially populated from dns seeds, perhaps updated in some way (again, independent of the node), bitcoind wallet sends private broadcast txs via bitcoin-privbcast's stdin, and then just monitors for them to appear in the mempool (and sends a cancel message to privbcast's stdin when that occurs), and bitcoin-privbcast rate limits, retries, expires them itself to avoid send bursts correlating with the node restarting.

That approach would allow people with higher or different tx privacy goals to replace the privbcast binary with something custom if desired (eg to make different tradeoffs about addr handling, or using tor exit nodes, etc), without needing to modify bitcoind source.

> The design doc looks AI written; is it meant for human or agentic consumption?

The PR text is AI written, curated a number of times under my direction as the primary document. I think there's great value for both humans and AI. It doesn't have to be in the merged branch.

> Shouldn't it be a BIP, or at least posted to the mailing list for broader discussion on exactly the sort of tradeoffs vasild raises https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6413061893?

I think there's definitely value increasing anonymity set if nothing else. By the same token, the current implementation should have gone through a BIP process, for exactly the same reasons.

> That approach 

Originally I designed it as a separate tool, but I was hoping for a like-for-like replacement. However the architecture lends itself just fine to it, as the only coupled code in this PR to the node is the queue portion. An "addrman but not node's addrman" is another design quest, because resisting cross-tx correlation, while a secondary goal, is worth trying to preserve under adversaries. 

> appear in the mempool (and sends a cancel message to privbcast's stdin when that occurs),

This is a leak. I prefer bounded tries. We could have it do retries based on block non-inclusion or some other criteria that isn't a clear fingerprint, e.g., not enough peers asking for the tx itself.

> Peers can be influenced, by design, into dialing to peers that are unique fingerprints, with the attacker writing to their addrman.

Can this design be expanded on about how they can be influenced, and why that is by design? Would this mean the problem is with the design that allows peers to be influenced into dialing to peers that are unique fingerprints, and not the actual private broadcast? Perhaps this can be solved by a better upstream design in addrman?

> Currently in master, it makes sybiling victims much easier, which results in an IP address leak

Would that be a problem with i2p in general, and not private broadcast? I'm not sure I understand how a sybil attack in i2p could leak a clearnet IP address.

How would sybiling the node affect sending private broadcast transactions through ephemeral i2p tunnels? These connections should not be connected in any way to the broadcasting node's long-lived i2p address (if it has one) or their tor onion address or clearnet addresses.

> The attacks it resists are quite limited today

Since we no longer make any promises, and this is marked experimental, can we elaborate on the attacks it cannot resist? I find it difficult to reason about the tradeoffs presented here with respect to attacks that I do not understand or know about. Similarly with the above claims about peer influence and i2p sybiling. Wasn't part of the benefit of marking experimental to allow these attacks and weaknesses to be discussed openly?

events.message:
doc: add the private broadcast specification

This is the design the following commits implement: what a private
broadcast job guarantees, the values peers and observers see, and the
node's interface. Later commits cite its items by number.

privbcast: add the parameters and the schedule

Start src/privbcast, the code that will run the node's private
broadcast jobs, built into bitcoin_node. params.h holds the values of
the specification. DrawPlan draws a job's plan from the job's own
randomness: the schedule, the order of the DNS seeds and the seed of
the order in which each DNS seed hands out its candidates.
MIN_DNS_SEEDS is the floor R3 sets for the mainnet seed list, and a
unit test holds the list to it, so a release that drops seeds below
what fills a job fails the test rather than leaving opportunities
empty.

Implements C1 and R3; the values of Parameters.

privbcast: add candidate assignment

Assign fixes every opportunity's candidate once discovery ends, from
the plan and the discovery result alone. An endpoint that several
seeds returned is credited to the seed that comes first in the plan's
seed order, through the lowest query set that returned it. Each seed
hands out its candidates in an order drawn at random by a generator of
its own, seeded from the plan and the seed's place in that order. Slot
j's first attempt comes from query set j mod 4 whenever a seed it may
draw from has one, so a single exit supplies at most two first
attempts. Neither which seed answers first nor the order of a seed's
answers changes the assignment.

Implements C2, R2, R4, R5a, R5b and R5c.

privbcast: add a byte-driven SOCKS5 client

A job reaches recipients and resolves DNS seed names through the proxy,
on streams its event loop drives without blocking. Socks5Client holds
no socket: it offers the bytes to write, consumes the proxy's replies,
and leaves bytes past the final reply to the P2P transport. It offers
only username and password authentication, with the credentials it is
given or fresh ones, and fails before sending anything if they are
outside RFC 1929's lengths or the username would select Tor's extended
parameters. It sends every destination as a name, numeric addresses
included, and resolves nothing: the node's own connections do the
same, and Tor's SafeSocks refuses a request that carries only an
address. Its errors name the proxy's reply with netbase's
Socks5ErrorString, now exported.

Implements B2 and the Proxy interface section.

privbcast: add the attempt state machine

An attempt is one connection to a recipient once the proxy connected
it: a BIP324 session as initiator, the handshake with the job's
VERSION, one INV, the transaction served at most once, and the PING.
It holds no socket and reads no clock: the job's loop passes the bytes
read and the time; each call records what happened (a completed write,
the connection, bytes received) and then enforces the attempt's
deadlines, so that nothing is acted on at or after one.

The attempt draws its VERSION and PING nonces from the random context
it is given, and takes its BIP324 key, ellswift entropy and garbage
from a key source. Without one, as in production, V2Transport draws
them from the strong RNG. The fuzz target injects a source
that draws from its seeded context, so that an attempt's bytes are a
function of that context and of what the peer sent.

Implements E1-E8, A2, B4, D3 and the attempt part of D2.

privbcast: add proxy streams and discovery

A job reaches the network only through streams to the SOCKS5 proxy,
which its event loop drives without blocking. ProxyStream connects to
the proxy by address or unix socket path, resolving nothing, and runs
the exchange of its Socks5Client; each stage, the connect and each
step of the exchange, times out on the steady clock. Once the proxy
has connected the stream, its socket carries the destination's bytes.

Discovery launches every RESOLVE query at job start, each on a stream
of its own, in four query sets: each set has credentials of its own
and one query of every seed, so Tor builds four circuits rather than
one per query, and each seed is still asked through four exits.
Discovery ends when every query has ended or when the discovery window
does, whatever is still pending. It keeps the answers that are public
routable IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, with the chain's default port, and
counts the others; its result gives each seed's answers by the query
set they came through, whatever order they arrived in. An exception
thrown while it acts on one query ends only that query, as a failed
stream would.

Implements B1, B2, C3, D1, R1, R2 and C7 for the queries.

privbcast: add the job

A job is one event loop on its caller's thread. Step() runs the
deadlines and the dials that are due, waits on every open stream until
the next deadline, and does the I/O; Run() steps to the end. The plan
is drawn when the job is made, before any socket exists, and discovery
starts with the first step. When discovery ends the assignment is
fixed, and each slot dials its opportunities at their scheduled times,
one attempt at a time, until one reaches the announcement point or
none is left; a job whose discovery found no candidate ends there,
failed with "no candidates". The slots share only the loop, so a stalled stream holds
up no other slot, and the cancel flag ends everything at the next step.

An exception thrown while the loop acts on one attempt ends only that
attempt, as a failed stream would. One thrown anywhere else in a step
fails the job: it stops as a cancelled job does, and its report gives
the error.

The report mirrors Interface/Report, every time an offset from job
start on the plan clock. Snapshot() gives the progress the node is to
show, from any thread.

Implements A1, A3, A4, C1-C8, D1, D2, H1-H3 and the report interface.

test: extend the harness for private broadcast jobs

The SOCKS5 server gains Tor's RESOLVE command, reply delays for a slow
or stalled proxy, a mode that offers only unauthenticated access and a
mode that behaves as an ordinary non-Tor proxy. A client that hangs up
before its greeting, as a cancelled job's streams can, and a connection
that Windows reports as aborted count as closed, not as errors. The P2P
network thread judges a failed protocol by its own reconnect flag, so
that several listeners can share one loop. test_framework/privbcast.py
holds the release's parameters, a scripted recipient, and the checks of
a job's wire profile, of fresh keys and nonces in each attempt, and of
its schedule, report summary and proxy credentials.

Prepares the functional tests of the node's jobs.

node: add the private broadcast job queue

The node runs each private broadcast as a privbcast::Job on a thread of
its own. PrivbcastQueue queues the submitted transactions, starts and
cancels the jobs from one scheduler thread, and keeps in memory the
records that getprivatebroadcastinfo and abortprivatebroadcast are to
show. It reaches the node only through callbacks for networking, the
onion proxy and the mempool, and takes the job runner as a parameter,
so that tests can drive it with stub jobs and mocked clocks. A job that
failed, or whose runner threw, ends aborted with the error in its
record. Whether a cancel cut a job short is read from its report, so
one that lands after the job ended leaves it done. At shutdown the
default log gives the number of jobs stopped, and nothing more.

The scheduler's start rule is a pure function, StartPolicy::Decide(),
which each pass of the scheduler applies.

Implements N3-N7, N9, N10, the node's D2 and D3, U3. Not yet wired:
the next commit switches -privatebroadcast to it.

node: run private broadcast as jobs

With -privatebroadcast, sendrawtransaction now queues a job on the
node's PrivbcastQueue instead of handing the transaction to the
connection manager, getprivatebroadcastinfo lists the jobs with their
progress and reports, and abortprivatebroadcast aborts them. Startup
requires onion to be able to become reachable, refuses the regtest
seed and time divisor overrides on other chains, on signet
-signetseednode and -signetchallenge, and off regtest a non-zero
-mocktime, requires -privatebroadcastseed on regtest, which has no DNS
seeds, and refuses to start rather than trim connections when the
jobs' file descriptors are not available. -connect and -proxyrandomize
no longer matter.

-privatebroadcasttimedivisor, regtest only, divides every duration of
a job's plan, so that functional tests can run jobs in real time.

The old private broadcast connections and relay stay in the tree, no
longer fed, until the commits that remove them.

Implements N1, N2, N8, N10, N11, U1, U2 and Interface/Node; replaces
the old implementation's tests with the specification's.

test: run private broadcast jobs end to end through the node

p2p_private_broadcast.py drives jobs on a mocked clock, which moves a
job's schedule but not the steady clock that times its proxy exchanges
and connections. These tests run jobs in real time instead, shortened
by -privatebroadcasttimedivisor: a recipient that floods a job is cut
off at the receive cap, and a proxy that refuses authentication or is
not Tor gets nothing to carry.

test_framework/privbcast.py gains the harness: it restarts the node
behind each scenario's SOCKS5 server with its seeds and time divisor,
and reads the job's report from getprivatebroadcastinfo.

net: remove the old private broadcast relay

Since -privatebroadcast runs jobs, nothing hands PeerManager a
transaction for private broadcast any more. Remove its queue
(src/private_broadcast.{h,cpp}) with the methods, the retry task and
the private_broadcast option that served it, and its handling of
private broadcast connections: the fixed VERSION, the INV after
VERACK, the GETDATA and PONG handling, the incoming message filter,
the lifetime limit and the exemption from discouragement. The unit and
fuzz tests of that code go with it, including the net_tests case for
the addrman exception and the denialofservice_tests cases for the
discouragement exemption.

Delete-only: besides whole lines, conditions and arguments are cut out
of lines, and the lines of a removed branch's alternative move out one
indentation level. git show -w --word-diff-regex='[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
shows deletions only, apart from the size of the node array in
denialofservice_tests, which goes back from 5 to 3.

net: remove the old private broadcast connections

With the relay gone, nothing asks CConnman for private broadcast
connections. Remove the connection type, the thread that opened such
connections with its counters and choice of network, and the places
that treated them specially: the incoming nonce check, the fresh I2P
session, the guard against direct connections, the outbound message
filter, the fixed protocol version, the exception in disconnection by
subnet and their term in the orphanage's static_assert. The type's
names go from getpeerinfo's help, bitcoin-cli -netinfo and the GUI. The
proxy override of ConnectNode() and OpenNetworkConnection(), which only
that thread set, goes too, with its copy in CNode and in the
reconnection record and the fuzz input for it.

Delete-only: besides whole lines, conditions, arguments and list
separators are cut out of lines, what followed a cut argument joins
its line, and one line moves out an indentation level with the if
around it. git show -w --word-diff-regex='[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
shows deletions only.

refactor: drop the trivial AdvertisedVersion()

Without private broadcast connections, a node advertises
PROTOCOL_VERSION on every connection, and CNode::AdvertisedVersion()
only returns it. Use the constant again where the method was called.

doc: describe bitcoind -privatebroadcast

Add the user guide to private broadcast: which Tor proxy the jobs use,
how sendrawtransaction queues them and when they start, what is not
queued again, how to follow and abort jobs, what disabling networking
and shutdown do, which node settings do not apply, what the default
log shows, the file descriptors the jobs need, and the limits of what
a job protects.
doc: release notes for private broadcast jobs

comments.body: 70016 is what current private broadcast versions track, and avoiding varying these things across releases is exactly why we have a special profile.
